rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the common tolerance reading, the verse expresses disgust, permanent severance from the disbelievers, and a declaration of war.
rows.anchor: Generally, people have regarded this verse to be an expression of tolerance. However, this verse actually expresses disgust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham and his followers are the example for the Prophet and his followers to disown their people, so the verse cannot express tolerance.
rows.anchor: The example of Abraham (sws) and his followers has only been presented before the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ignoring discourse context makes readers confuse words of disgust with words of tolerance; this verse illustrates that failure.
rows.anchor: This verse is a very good example of this failure

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following the severance proclaimed in al-Kāfirūn, al-Naṣr foretells imminent divine aid, the conquest of Mecca, and completion of the Prophet's mission.
rows.anchor: glad tidings are given to the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At migration the message has been fully conveyed, the faithful form an organized community, and the ensuing conflict ends in God's victory after trials.
rows.anchor: when the time of migration comes in the life of the messengers the truth has been communicated to their people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although one view dates the sūrah after Mecca's conquest and another before it as its glad tidings, Islahi prefers the latter.
rows.anchor: I would pr efer the second of these.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Liberating the Baytullāh, the center of Abraham's religion, was the Prophet's final real mission; other achievements were its by-products.
rows.anchor: hence liberating it from people who violated its trust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Breaking Quraysh's power was the real victory because its custodianship of the Baytullāh gave it authority and awe throughout Arabia.
rows.anchor: To break the shackles of their power was real victory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised aid is God's established victory for His messengers, the same promise stated in al-Mujādalah and al-Ṣaff.
rows.anchor: a consequence of the promise of the Almighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The victory can only mean Mecca's conquest; those who date the sūrah after it have misunderstood a narrative.
rows.anchor: the victory and help mentioned in this sūrah is the conquest of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah promises Mecca's liberation, mass conversion, and success in the Prophet's mission; that final glad tiding signals his death is near.
rows.anchor: the time of the Prophet’s death is also near

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās inferred from this part of the sūrah that the Prophet's death was near.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi calls Ibn ʿAbbās's inference subtle and says ʿUmar praised and corroborated it.
rows.anchor: No doubt this was a subtle inference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic reference is to the messengers' divinely promised victory, granted after they exhaust communication and their people persist in denial and hostility.
rows.anchor: when a Messenger has exhausted all ways of communication in delivering his message to his people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article on al-fatḥ marks the promised victory of God's established practice; the phrase elsewhere likewise means Mecca's conquest.
rows.anchor: the promised victory which comes to the messengers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conquest of Mecca is uniquely called the victory because it measures deeds before and after it and ended Arabia's capacity to oppose Islam.
rows.anchor: Before the conquest of Makkah, Muslims had achieved victory on numerous occasions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the conquest sermon, the Prophet addressed Quraysh leaders who had fought him and were now prisoners awaiting judgment.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) turned his attention to the leaders and pundits of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: Prophet (sws)
rows.claim: When the captured Quraysh leaders expected judgment, the Prophet told them to go free after they called him a noble brother.
rows.anchor: After hearing this reply, the Prophet (sws) said: “Go now, you are free.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since victory comes only through God's help, the victor must not boast of personal skill but credit God and praise Him with gratitude.
rows.anchor: not befitting for a person to show vanity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conflict was religious: Quraysh had no right to retain the House or use coercion to stop people embracing God's religion, so the Prophet removed them.
rows.anchor: they had no right to keep it in their custody

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh threatened Anṣār pledging allegiance with war against Arabs and non-Arabs; after its coercive climate ended, people could accept Islam freely.
rows.anchor: this pledge was tantamount to declaring war on

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mecca's conquest ended Quraysh's terror and transformed Arabia, allowing mass conversion; no other victory had this result.
rows.anchor: This is a very strong testimony that the victory referred to here is the conquest of Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After divine aid and Mecca's conquest, the Prophet and Companions should glorify God, thank Him, and seek forgiveness rather than take pride, as taught by al-Kawthar.
rows.anchor: seek forgiveness from Him for their sins

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Victory entails duties: keeping them sustains God's blessings, while neglect brings their withdrawal or severe trials.

rows.claim: Prophets do not sin from base desire; blemishes arise when noble motives make them exceed limits, as Muhammad overstrained himself to reform rebels unworthy of such effort.
rows.anchor: stopped from over trying and straining himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Fatḥ states the same glad tidings more explicitly: victory brings forgiveness for past and future blemishes, completion of favor, and guidance.

rows.claim: Tasbīḥ absolves God of what is unworthy of His majesty.
rows.anchor: to absolve the Almighty of all

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamd asserts the attributes God truly possesses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most exegetes call al-Lahab Makkan because it answered Abū Lahab's insult at Ṣafā, but Islahi says this dating argument is unsound.
rows.anchor: Most exegetes regard it to be a Makkan sūrah

rows.speaker: Exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes report that at Ṣafā the Prophet warned his gathered Quraysh relatives of punishment and Abū Lahab retorted with a curse; they say this occasioned the sūrah.
rows.anchor: Exegetes say that it is this incident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi accepts that the incident occurred but says it is improbable that the sūrah answered Abū Lahab and his wife's misconduct.
rows.anchor: for various reasons it is improbable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revealed phrase is no tit-for-tat curse; Islahi says it carries no ring of condemnation.
rows.anchor: These words in no way have a ring of condemnation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening predicts the end of Abū Lahab's political dominance, the defeat of his allies, and the loss of his pomp and wealth.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening is a prediction rather than a statement of a present fact.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since Abū Lahab died shortly after Badr, Islahi dates the prediction around that period and before his death.
